merge_ruling.for_merge: The poll filed 11 August 1834 prints 'Paine, William' (voter_lists_1833_1835.txt line 254) and the Chicago Democrat of 13 August 1834 prints 'Wm. Payne' — one forename, one letter of surname, four days apart, in a town of some hundreds. Neither card carries a trade, an address or a second forename that the other contradicts.
merge_ruling.against_merge: PAINE AND PAYNE ARE BOTH POPULATED SURNAMES IN THIS CORPUS AND THIS TOWN, WHICH IS WHAT THE OTHER NINE PAIRS ARE NOT. The town already holds Seth Paine beside William Paine, and L. W. Payne beside William Payne — two bearers of each spelling, ruled apart by their own forenames. The 1835 poll enters 'Payne, L. W.' (line 343) while the 1834 poll enters 'Paine, William' (line 254), so the town's rolls carry both surnames in their own right. The post office's list of 30 June 1835 prints THREE Paynes in one column — 'Payne Barney', 'Payne Barrey W.', 'Payne Win.' — and no Paine at all. Fergus 1843 prints Paine five times and Payne never; Norris 1844 prints Paine five times. No title reached is caught setting both spellings for one WILLIAM, and where two surnames each have several live bearers a one-letter distance is at its weakest, not its strongest — it is the case T-1001's measurement was about. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.
